issues.issue: The named REINSURED is replaced by Amendment No. 3 (name change to OHIC Insurance Company), so the identity of the contracting party shifts across the instrument. The substitution is express, so little is left to construe.

The stated effective date of January 1, 1994 sits against Amendment No. 4(A), which rewrites Article I so the agreement applies to policies becoming effective on or after October 1, 1996, and against the cover page's 1996 date. Which inception date governs a given cession is not spelled out.

"Excess of underlying insurance which afford limits not less than the limits specified" leaves open whether a self-insured retention counts as "underlying insurance" and what happens if the underlying limits fall short. The phrase is a condition of attachment with no stated consequence for non-compliance.

The Schedule measures Hospital Professional Liability underlying limits by "each medical incident" while Article III (c009) and Amendment No. 4 (c080, c083) cap the reinsurance by "each occurrence," leaving the relationship between medical incidents, occurrences and claims unresolved.

"[S]ubject to the provision that a separate Limit of liability may apply in respect thereof" is permissive and unspecified: it does not say whose limit, when it applies, or whether a fresh reinsurance limit is created for the discovery/extended reporting period. That directly bears on how much the reinsurer owes.

"[T]eaching hospital, children's hospital or psychiatric hospital" in (a) are undefined even though the very next exclusion carefully defines "total beds," so the reach of (a) (e.g. a hospital with a small residency program) is open. Exclusion (g), "business to the extent that it is reinsured outside of this agreement," is likewise unbounded.

"$10,000,000 annual aggregate" does not say whether the aggregate runs per ceded policy, per hospital risk, or across all cessions in a treaty year, and "each occurrence" is undefined. Both are the classic reinsurance aggregation questions.

Amendment No. 1 and Amendment No. 4 each purport to delete Article III outright while applying only to policies effective on or after July 1, 1995 and October 1, 1996 respectively, so which limit ($10M or $25M) governs 1994–1996 cessions is unresolved.

The proviso is triggered when the underlying Hospital Professional Liability limit "of $1,000,000/$3,000,000" is self-insured, but it then describes the self-insured layer as $1,000,000 each occurrence/$1,000,000 annual aggregate — a mismatch with the $3,000,000 underlying aggregate. The $93,000,000 aggregate figure is also plainly a mis-writing of $9,000,000.

"Loss" is confined to amounts "actually paid by the REINSURED" and "within applicable policy limits," yet sub-paragraph (b) covers amounts paid in excess of policy limits, so the opening restriction and the enumerated items pull against each other. Whether payment must precede the reinsurer's obligation is left open.

"[A]llocated investigation, adjustment, and legal expenses" and "the supplementary payments provisions of the REINSURED'S policy" are undefined, so the line between allocated (reimbursable) and unallocated expense is left to argument. The "including" list is illustrative, not exhaustive.

The proviso indemnifies claim expenses "connected with such settlement or appeal," but no settlement is mentioned anywhere in the proviso — the antecedent is missing, so what expenses fall inside the special ratio is uncertain. The main pro-rata formula also does not say whether claim expenses sit within or in addition to the Article III limits.

The premium is fixed by "the Rating Schedule, attached hereto," but that schedule was replaced twice (Rating Schedule-A by Amendment No. 1, Rating Schedule-B by Amendment No. 4), so which schedule rates a given cession depends on reading the amendments together.

The operative sentence fixing the contingent commission is incomplete and unreadable as it appears, so the rate and base of the commission cannot be determined from the provision itself. Nothing in the text supplies the missing terms.

The provision says accounting periods run twenty-four months from every other January 1st, yet the final period on an off-cycle termination "shall commence on the fifth January 1st preceding the termination date" — a period of up to five years, inconsistent with the two-year rule in the same sentence. The intervening clause dealing with termination coinciding with an accounting period is also incomplete.

This requires the CORPORATION to pay the full contingent commission whenever a computation shows a net profit, but c030 provides that no further contingent commission shall be paid until all premium is earned and all losses paid. The two payment triggers cannot both operate after termination.

The credit is "written premium on reinsurance reported by the REINSURED," which does not say whether unearned, uncollected or subsequently returned premium is included, and the second credit item is unnumbered. The mismatch with the charge side (paid and unpaid losses) is left unaddressed.

The enumerated charges are mis-numbered and it is unclear whether losses paid in a later accounting period but attributable to an earlier period's claims are charged to the earlier period on the annual re-computations. The 15% home office overhead charge is keyed to "Item i of Credits to Profits," an item that is itself unnumbered in c025.

"[T]he reserve of individual cases as developed to the date the computation is made" does not say whose reserves control (the REINSURED's or the CORPORATION's) or whether IBNR is included. The figure directly drives the contingent commission.

"Net profit" is defined here treaty-wide as credits over charges, but Amendment No. 1 (c065) promises 40% of net profit "accruing to the REINSURED" limited to the first $1,000,000 of reinsured limits per policy — a base this definition does not supply.

The bar on paying "further contingent commission ... until all the reinsurance premium ... shall have been earned and all losses for which the CORPORATION is liable shall have been paid" cannot be squared with c024, which requires payment of the full commission whenever a computation shows a net profit, nor with c023's annual re-computations.

"[A] bordereau on a form satisfactory to the CORPORATION" gives one party an unbounded standard for the cedent's reporting obligation, and the provision does not say what the bordereau must contain. The consequence of an unsatisfactory or late bordereau is unstated.

"The amount due the CORPORATION" is not defined or tied to the bordereau, and the sentence makes no provision for balances running the other way. Whether ceding and contingent commissions are netted here is left open.

"[P]rompt notice ... of any event or development which might result in a claim upon the CORPORATION" is vague at both ends — "prompt" is unmeasured and "might result" sets no threshold of likelihood — and no consequence for late notice is stated. Late-notice is precisely the kind of standard two reinsurance parties read differently.

"[I]n the judgment of the CORPORATION" commits the trigger for joint participation to one party's opinion, and "participate jointly" does not say who controls the defence or settlement. Its fit with the REINSURED's duty to settle or defend under c033 is left to inference.

"[P]romptly" and "satisfactory evidence of payment of such loss" are both unmeasured, and the second leaves the reinsurer to judge the sufficiency of the cedent's proof. Nothing says what happens if evidence is withheld as unsatisfactory.

The sentence is garbled and incomplete — the CORPORATION "will furnish to the REINSURED the CORPORATION'S payment of loss ... on the ... date on which the REINSURED proposes to make payment" — so the mechanics and timing of pre-funding cannot be read off the text. It also sits awkwardly with c035's requirement of evidence of payment already made.

The unrestricted right to offset balances under "any other reinsurance agreement" pulls against the Insolvency Clause (c054), which requires reinsurance to be payable without diminution because of the cedent's insolvency.

The Stipulation of Termination (c103) ends the treaty by reference to policies issued on or after January 1, 1998 rather than by the mutual-consent or 90-day-notice mechanism this article prescribes, leaving the interaction of the two unstated.

The 12-months-plus-odd-time cap on post-termination run-off cannot be squared with the very next sentence (c041), which continues cover for discovery period coverages and extended reporting endorsements without any such cap, nor with c006, which folds those periods into the policy period.

This continues cover for extended reporting endorsements attaching to policies in force at cancellation without limit of time, while c040 caps continued cover at 12 months plus odd time; c006 adds that a separate limit of liability "may" apply. The three cannot be harmonised on how long and to what limit run-off cover lasts.

Sub-paragraph (iv) turns on "substantial quantities of radioactive isotopes," an unquantified threshold, although c048 makes the REINSURED sole judge of what is substantial. The residual category "installations other than those listed" is also open-ended.

The carve-out "except that this paragraph (3) shall not operate" runs into two conditions whose text is fragmentary, so the scope of the exception to the radioactive-contamination exclusion cannot be read off the provision. The 1960 proviso adds a further undated condition.

The carve-out turns on the nuclear exposure not being "considered by the REINSURED to be the primary hazard," a subjective and unmeasured test applied by the party seeking cover. Nothing states how that judgment is reviewed.

The grandfathering of policies issued on or before 31 December 1957 has no possible application in a treaty effective January 1, 1994 covering only policies becoming effective on or after that date (Article I).
Like c049, the 1958 Canadian grandfathering cannot apply to any policy within Article I's scope, which is limited to policies becoming effective on or after January 1, 1994.

The deeming provision imports a "Limited Exclusion Provision" into classes of original policies (family automobile, homeowners and similar personal lines) that a hospital excess liability treaty would never cede. Its text is also fragmentary in places.
